description: Food miles, packaging, carbon footprint and waste, plus the global challenge of food security and Fairtrade.
content_html:
Food and the Environment

The food on your plate has already travelled a long journey — sometimes thousands of miles. Every stage of that journey, from the farm to the factory to the shop shelf, leaves an environmental mark. Understanding those marks — and what we can do about them — is an increasingly important part of food literacy.

Food Miles and Carbon Footprint

Food miles measure how far food travels from farm to fork. A bag of runner beans flown from Kenya to a UK supermarket generates far more carbon dioxide than the same beans grown in a British garden in summer. Carbon footprint is the broader measure — it accounts for all greenhouse gas emissions associated with producing, processing, packaging and transporting food.

Buying seasonal food reduces both food miles and carbon footprint. British strawberries in June travel a short distance and need no artificial growing conditions. The same strawberries imported from Spain in December required heated glasshouses and long-haul lorry transport, dramatically increasing their carbon footprint. Choosing seasonal and local food where possible is one of the most practical steps a consumer can take.

Key Fact

Food miles measure the distance food travels from farm to consumer. Buying seasonal and locally produced food reduces food miles, lowers carbon dioxide emissions from transport, and reduces the need for energy-intensive glasshouse growing.

Packaging and Environmental Issues

Food packaging serves essential functions: it protects food from contamination, extends shelf life, provides labelling information and enables safe transport. However, excessive packaging — particularly single-use plastics — creates significant environmental problems. Much plastic packaging ends up in landfill or water systems where it takes hundreds of years to break down. Glass and cardboard are more recyclable but heavier to transport, increasing fuel use. Retailers and manufacturers are under growing pressure to reduce packaging, switch to recycled materials, and design packaging that can be collected and reused.

When evaluating packaging in your exam, avoid saying it is simply “bad”. Packaging prevents food waste (which also has a carbon cost), keeps food safe from bacterial contamination, and makes transport practical. A balanced exam answer weighs the environmental cost of the packaging material against the food waste it prevents. For example: a plastic film on a prepared salad extends shelf life by several days, potentially saving more environmental damage than it causes — provided the plastic is recycled. The written paper rewards this kind of nuanced, both-sides reasoning.

Food Waste

Food waste occurs at every stage of the supply chain: on the farm (produce left unharvested because it doesn’t meet cosmetic standards), during processing and retail (products approaching use-by dates), and in the home. Households throw away approximately 9.5 million tonnes of food waste per year in the UK, much of which is still edible. Wasted food represents wasted energy, water and labour. Rotting food in landfill also produces methane, a potent greenhouse gas. Practical ways to reduce household food waste include meal planning, correct food storage, using leftovers creatively (a Sunday roast chicken provides stock, sandwiches and stir-fry meat for days), and freezing food before it reaches its use-by date.

Key Fact

Reducing food waste saves money, conserves the energy and water used to produce food, and cuts methane emissions from landfill decomposition. Practical strategies include meal planning, correct storage, creative use of leftovers and freezing food before it spoils.

Food Security: a Global Challenge

Food security means everyone having reliable access to enough safe, nutritious and affordable food. Global food security is under increasing pressure from several interconnected challenges.

Climate change and global warming are shifting growing seasons and making weather patterns less predictable. Regions that once reliably produced wheat or maize are experiencing unpredictable frosts, heat waves and unseasonal rainfall. Drought and flooding directly destroy crops and make farmland unusable. Extreme drought in East Africa has repeatedly caused harvest failures and food crises in recent decades. Flooding in low-lying delta regions such as Bangladesh regularly destroys rice crops.

A growing global population puts more pressure on finite agricultural land. The world population is expected to reach around 10 billion by 2050, meaning food production will need to increase substantially on roughly the same area of farmland. Insufficient land for growing food is worsened by urbanisation, soil degradation and water scarcity.

Food poverty is specifically about affordability and access at the individual or household level — a person is in food poverty if they cannot afford or physically access a nutritious diet. Food security is a broader concept that covers availability at national and global scale. A country can have food security (enough food is produced or imported) while individuals within it experience food poverty (they cannot afford it). In your exam, use the correct term for the correct scale of problem.

Fairtrade and GM Foods as Responses

Fairtrade is a certification scheme that guarantees farmers in developing countries a minimum fair price for their produce — whether coffee, cocoa, bananas or cotton. The Fairtrade premium also funds community projects such as schools and clean water. Buying Fairtrade products directly supports food security and sustainable livelihoods in some of the world’s most vulnerable farming communities. Genetically modified (GM) foods are also proposed as a response to food security challenges: drought-tolerant GM crops, for example, could maintain yields in regions where conventional varieties would fail. However, concerns about biodiversity, corporate control of the seed supply and long-term health effects mean GM remains controversial as a food security strategy.
exam_tip_html: On a 9-mark Analyse question about food security, the key mistake is describing the challenges rather than analysing them. “Analyse” means breaking the topic into parts and examining relationships and consequences. Rather than listing “climate change causes droughts”, examine the chain: climate change → unpredictable rainfall patterns → crop failures in regions dependent on specific growing seasons → localised food insecurity → price spikes that hit the poorest hardest. Then consider how a response (Fairtrade, GM, sustainable farming) addresses that specific chain. Top-band answers examine multiple challenges, explore the links between them, and evaluate how effectively different responses address each. Use specific geographical examples where you can, but invented detail is not needed — general but developed reasoning earns marks.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Food miles and carbon footprint measure the environmental cost of transporting food; seasonal and locally bought food reduces both, while packaging trade-offs must be weighed against the food waste it prevents.
  • Food waste occurs across the supply chain and at home; reducing it saves money and cuts methane emissions from landfill.
  • Food security — reliable access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food — is threatened globally by climate change, drought, flooding, a growing population and insufficient farmland; Fairtrade and GM crops are among the proposed responses.

practice_questions.text:
What does the term 'food miles' measure?
A. The nutritional value of food per kilogram
B. The distance food travels from production to the consumer
C. The weight of packaging used to transport food
D. The number of countries a food product passes through
State two environmental problems caused by excessive food packaging.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each of two acceptable problems from: plastic waste in landfill or water systems; non-biodegradable materials taking hundreds of years to break down; increased transport weight requiring more fuel; contribution to greenhouse gas emissions during manufacture; litter and wildlife harm. Maximum 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe three challenges to global food security.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each of three distinct challenges described with relevant detail: climate change/global warming disrupting growing seasons (1); drought and flooding destroying crops (1); growing global population increasing demand on finite farmland (1); insufficient or degraded land for growing food (1); food waste reducing available supply (1). Any three, each with sufficient description. Maximum 3 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain how Fairtrade supports food security and sustainable livelihoods for farmers in developing countries.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. Guarantee of a minimum fair price (1) because it protects farmers from price volatility in global markets, meaning they have stable income to invest in their farms (1). Fairtrade premium funds community infrastructure such as schools, healthcare and clean water (1) which improves living conditions and enables communities to sustain agricultural production long-term (1). Two developed explanations linking the mechanism to the consequence required for full marks.

practice_questions.text: A secondary school is developing a sustainability policy for its canteen. The canteen currently sources most ingredients from a large national distributor, uses significant single-use plastic packaging, and throws away a substantial amount of prepared food each day. Analyse the environmental impact of the canteen's current food practices and suggest how each could be improved.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–9): Identifies all three issues (sourcing, packaging, waste) and analyses each with a developed chain of environmental consequences. Sourcing: national distributor means high food miles and associated carbon dioxide emissions; switching to local/seasonal suppliers reduces transport emissions and supports local economy. Packaging: single-use plastic contributes to landfill, water pollution and slow breakdown; switching to recyclable or biodegradable materials and reducing portion sizes of packaging reduces environmental harm. Waste: daily prepared food waste produces methane in landfill and wastes the energy/water used in production; solutions include better demand forecasting, smaller batch cooking, donating near-date food, composting unavoidable waste. Analysis examines relationships between the issues (e.g. better sourcing also reduces packaging needs) and evaluates the practical feasibility of solutions. Accurate use of terminology (food miles, carbon footprint, food waste, sustainability) throughout.

Secure (5–6): Addresses at least two issues with developed analysis. Generally accurate. Links issues to environmental consequences. Solutions present but may be limited.

Developing (3–4): Identifies issues with limited development. One-sided or descriptive. Points stated without clear consequence chain.

Emerging (1–2): Basic identification of one or two issues. Little or no environmental analysis. Vague suggestions.

practice_questions.text: Name one specific strategy a household could use to reduce food waste at home.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: meal planning before shopping; correct food storage (fridge/freezer temperatures); freezing food before use-by date; using leftovers creatively; buying only what is needed; checking use-by and best-before dates when shopping.

knowledge_checks.q: Which term describes the total greenhouse gas emissions associated with producing, processing and transporting a food product?
What does Fairtrade certification guarantee for farmers in developing countries?
options: Free transport of their produce to the UK
A minimum fair and stable price for their goods
A reduction in food miles on their products
Government subsidies to reduce production costs

knowledge_checks.q: Food security exists when all people have physical and economic access to sufficient, safe and _____ food.
Rotting food in landfill produces _____, a potent greenhouse gas that contributes to climate change.
Match each food and environment term with its correct meaning.
right: Inability to afford a healthy diet due to low income
Distance food travels from farm to consumer
Total greenhouse gas emissions of a food product
Reliable access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food

flashcard_questions.a: The distance food travels from its point of production to the consumer.
The total greenhouse gas emissions produced by an activity, product or person.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does buying seasonal food reduce carbon footprint?
flashcard_questions.a: Less transport distance and no need for energy-intensive glasshouse growing.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one environmental problem caused by excessive single-use plastic packaging.
flashcard_questions.a: Plastic in landfill or waterways takes hundreds of years to break down.
When all people have reliable access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food to meet their dietary needs.

flashcard_questions.q: How does food poverty differ from food insecurity?
flashcard_questions.a: Food poverty is inability to afford a nutritious diet; food security is the broader global supply question.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two climate-related threats to global food security.
flashcard_questions.a: Drought and flooding destroy crops; unpredictable growing seasons from climate change.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Fairtrade guarantee to farmers in developing countries?
flashcard_questions.a: A minimum fair and stable price for their produce.

flashcard_questions.q: How does the Fairtrade premium benefit farming communities beyond the price guarantee?
flashcard_questions.a: It funds community development projects — schools, healthcare, clean water — improving long-term livelihoods.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one gas produced by food rotting in landfill.
Give one practical way a household can reduce food waste.
flashcard_questions.a: Meal plan before shopping to buy only what is needed.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is a growing global population a challenge for food security?
flashcard_questions.a: More people need feeding from roughly the same amount of finite farmland.

glossary_terms.definition: A measure of the distance food travels from its point of production to the consumer, used as an indicator of the environmental cost of transportation.
The total amount of greenhouse gases, expressed as equivalent tonnes of carbon dioxide, produced by an activity, product or person.
The condition in which all people, at all times, have physical and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food to meet their dietary needs.
The inability to afford or access a healthy and nutritious diet, typically as a result of low income.
A certification scheme that ensures producers in developing countries receive a fair and stable price for their goods, supporting sustainable livelihoods.
